title: SMTP Service Extension for 8-bit MIME Transport
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets message bodies with octets outside US-ASCII be relayed directly. It obsoletes RFC 1652 and is a standard.

eli5.summary: Old email could only carry plain English letters. This lets mail servers say they can carry other characters safely.

questions: what does body=8bitmime do in smtp
what happens if a server does not support 8bitmime
subtitle: How an SMTP server announces that it will accept 8-bit MIME message bodies, and how a client asks to send one.

tldr.problem: SMTP was built for 7-bit US-ASCII text, but many people wanted to exchange MIME messages containing arbitrary octet-aligned material.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises the 8BITMIME keyword in its EHLO reply, and the client adds BODY=8BITMIME (or BODY=7BIT) to the MAIL command.
tldr.outcome: A server that accepts such a body must preserve every bit, and a client must never send 8-bit content to a server that did not advertise the extension. This memo obsoletes RFC 1652.

today: RFC 6152 is an Internet Standard (STD 71) and obsoletes RFC 1652. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this unit.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMTP is widely deployed, but parts of the Internet community wanted to exchange messages whose body is a MIME message holding arbitrary octet-aligned material. RFC 6152 uses the extension mechanism of RFC 5321 to define a way to do that.

It sets a limit up front. The extension does not stop a server from limiting line length, and servers may still set a limit no lower than 1000 octets. So it does not provide a way to transfer unencoded binary over SMTP.
sections.eli5: Email used to allow only plain letters. This note adds a polite way to ask for more characters, but it is still not a way to send any file as-is.

sections.title: Framework of the Extension
sections.content:
The extension is named 8bit-MIMEtransport. Its EHLO keyword is 8BITMIME, and that keyword takes no parameter. No new SMTP verbs are added.

The only addition is one optional parameter on the MAIL command, BODY. Its value says what kind of content follows: 7BIT for a message in strict compliance with RFC 5321, or 8BITMIME for a MIME message (in strict compliance with RFC 2046 and RFC 2045) with arbitrary octet content. The syntax is body-value = "7BIT" / "8BITMIME".
sections.eli5: The server holds up a sign saying 8BITMIME. The sender then adds a note to the envelope saying whether the letter inside is plain or fancy.

sections.title: Negotiating and Using the Extension
sections.content:
A client first sends EHLO. If the server answers with code 250 and the response includes 8BITMIME, the server is saying it supports the extended MAIL command and will accept MIME messages with arbitrary octet-aligned material.

The extended MAIL command is the same as in RFC 5321, except that a BODY parameter must appear after the address, and only one BODY parameter may be used in a single command.

A server that supports the extension shall preserve all bits in each octet passed using DATA. Once it accepts a body with the high-order (8th) bit set, it must deliver or relay the content so that all bits are preserved. The usual data-stuffing still applies, so a lone dot line cannot end the transfer early, and the CR-LF pair just before the final dot is part of the content.

Line length limits still apply, and may allow as few as 1000 octets including the CR-LF. The extension carries MIME objects with the 8BIT content-transfer-encoding, but it does not carry the BINARY encoding.
sections.eli5: First ask, 'Can you take special characters?' Only if the answer is yes do you send them. Once the server says yes, it promises not to scramble a single bit.

sections.title: When the Server Does Not Support It
sections.content:
If the server does not answer EHLO with code 250, or leaves 8BITMIME out of its reply, the client must not, under any circumstances, try to transfer content with characters outside the US-ASCII octet range (hex 00-7F).

The client then has two options. It may convert the message to valid 7-bit MIME in a gateway transformation, or it may treat the barrier to 8-bit as a permanent error and handle it as a normal delivery failure. The RFC does not describe how to convert, but requires that the conversion cause no loss of information (using MIME transport encodings as needed) and that the result be valid 7-bit MIME.
sections.eli5: If the server does not say it can handle special characters, you must not send them. You can either rewrite the message in plain letters or tell the sender it could not be delivered.

sections.title: A Usage Example
sections.content: The RFC gives a short dialogue. The server answers EHLO with a multi-line 250 reply that ends in 8BITMIME. The client then sends MAIL FROM with BODY=8BITMIME, names a recipient with RCPT TO, sends DATA, and finishes with a line holding only a dot.
sections.eli5: The dialogue is a short chat: 'Hello, can you do 8-bit?' 'Yes.' 'Here is a letter that uses it.' 'Got it, thanks.'

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC does not discuss security issues and is not believed to raise any beyond those already endemic in email and present in fully conforming RFC 5321 implementations, including attacks helped by an option negotiation mechanism. Since MIME semantics are transport-neutral, 8BITMIME adds no more ability to spread malware than unextended 7-bit SMTP.

For IANA, the 8BITMIME entry in the SMTP Service Extensions registry was updated to point at this document, with the description 'SMTP and Submit transport of 8-bit MIME content'.
sections.eli5: Allowing more characters does not give bad guys any new tricks, so the note adds no new security worries.
